11-1

Lecture 11-1

Why does a real vessel not behave like plug flow or mixed flow — and what do we need to know about it?

Channeling & dead zonesMicrofluid / macrofluidEarly or late mixing

Lecture 11-1

Three things that decide how a fluid is contacted

  1. Ideal and industrial reactorsWhy large vessels drift from the ideals.
  2. Where real flow goes wrongVelocity profiles, short-circuits, dead zones.
  3. What we actually need to knowNot a velocity map — only how long fluid stays.
  4. State of aggregationMolecules that intermix, or clumps that never do.
  5. Earliness of mixingWhy it barely matters for one feed and decides two.

Every rate we have met sits somewhere on one map. Non-ideal flow has its own branch.

Rate in a chemical reactor

Non-ideal flow is a momentum-transfer effect

Ideal reactors · what each one assumes

Batch, mixed flow, plug flow

Ideal batch (BR)

Perfectly mixed: no concentration or temperature profile.

Mixed flow (MFR)

Outlet = contents. Needs a short mixing time: easy in a small vessel, not in an industrial one.

Plug flow (PFR)

No axial mixing with fluid ahead or behind; perfect mixing across $r$ and $\theta$. Approached in turbulent flow.

Industrial vessels are large and often not turbulent, so they drift from both.

From the textbook catalogue to the plant

Ideal reactors versus real ones

IdealReal reactors
Tubular familyplug-flow reactortubular, serpentine coil, fixed bed, tubular exchanger, fired heater, radial-flow, riser
Tank familywell-mixed reactorstirred tanks, sparged tank, lift-tube, bubbling fluidized bed

Each real reactor is designed as one ideal, then checked against how its fluid actually flows.

Every design so far assumed one of two flow patterns.

Where we start

Plug flow and mixed flow

  • One or the other is often the optimum, whatever we design for.
  • Both are simple to treat.
Real equipment always deviates from both. How do we account for that?

Levenspiel Fig. 11.1, redrawn

Four ways real flow departs from the ideal

Each one lowers the performance of a reactor, exchanger or packed column — so we must be able to detect it.

Deviations from plug flow

Same tube, different residence times

Any velocity profile gives different residence times, so different exit conversions.

  • Packed bed: radial and axial dispersion.
  • Short and long paths around particles, plus wall channelling.

A full velocity map would predict all of this, but measuring one is impractical.

Lowering the ambition

We only need how long each element stays

  • Different routes take different times to cross the vessel.
  • The distribution of those times in the exit stream is the residence time distribution (RTD).
  • A stimulus–response experiment measures it directly: inject tracer, watch the outlet.
To characterise a vessel: steady flow of one fluid, no reaction, no density change (Danckwerts, 1953).

Same volume, same flow — yet the spread of stay times tells plug, mixed, short-circuit and dead zone apart.

The spread of stay times is one factor. Two more decide how a real reactor performs.

The contacting pattern

Three interrelated factors

1 · RTD

How long the flowing elements stay in the vessel.

2 · Aggregation

Whether molecules move freely, or travel together in clumps.

3 · Earliness of mixing

Whether elements mix near the inlet or near the outlet.

This section meets each qualitatively; 11-2 to 11-5 measure the RTD, 11-6 and 11-7 read faults from it.

Factor 2 · state of aggregation

Two extremes: microfluid and macrofluid

  • Single-phase systems lie between the extremes.
  • A macrofluid packet never exchanges material with its neighbours: each one is a little batch reactor.
Hold onto “little batch reactor” — the segregation model builds its conversion equation on it.

Levenspiel Fig. 11.3, redrawn

In two phases, the contactor decides which is which

  • A stream of solids always behaves as a macrofluid.
  • Gas and liquid can each be either — the dispersed phase is the macrofluid.

Two-phase reactors are treated in later chapters; here we only name the behaviour.

State of aggregation · compare the two clocks

Micro or macro: set by reaction time against mixing time

Aggregation matters only when $n\ne1$: in mixed flow a macrofluid gives higher $X$ for $n>1$, lower for $n<1$.

Factor 3 · earliness of mixing · Fig. 11.4

Where along the vessel do elements mix?

For a single flowing fluid this factor usually has little effect on the overall behaviour.

Why this matters for non-ideal flow: the RTD cannot see when fluid mixes.

Earliness of mixing · the limit of a tracer test

Same RTD, different conversion when $n\ne1$

Equal plug and mixed volumesA: lateB: early
$n=1$, $k\tau_i=1$ in each$X=0.816$$X=0.816$
$n=2$, $kC_{A0}\tau_i=2$ in each$X=0.771$$X=0.750$

$\tau_i$: space time of each part. For $n=2$, A puts the plug first while $C_A$ is high.

The tracer sees one RTD; the reaction sees two reactors. For $n>1$ late mixing wins, for $n<1$ early mixing wins; $n=1$ does not care.

With two entering reactant streams, the same factor stops being minor.

Fig. 11.5 · A and B fed separately

Mixing decides whether A and B ever meet

Same vessel volume, same RTD — conversion anywhere from high to zero, set only by where A meets B.

Three time scales

Which factor can be ignored depends on the clock

$\bar t_{rx}$
time needed for reaction
s
$\bar t_{mix}$
time for elements to mix with each other
s
$\bar t_{stay}$
time spent in the vessel, close to $\bar t$
s
  • Mixing far faster than reaction: aggregation and earliness hardly matter.
  • Mixing as slow as reaction: all three factors decide the outcome.

Lecture 11-1

What section 11-1 settled

  • Short-circuits, dead zones, channels and recycle all lower performance — and change how long fluid stays.
  • We do not need a velocity map: the RTD, measured by tracer, is usually enough.
  • Microfluids intermix; macrofluids travel as packets that act like little batch reactors.
  • Early or late mixing barely matters for one feed and decides everything for two.

11-1 said a real vessel is described by how long fluid stays. A tracer measures exactly that.

Determination of RTD

Label the fluid, then watch it leave

  • Feed a physical, nonreactive tracer with the flow: it labels fluid without changing it.
  • Measure the tracer concentration at the reactor exit against time: the stimulus–response.

Absorbance

a coloured dye

Fluorescence

a fluorescent dye

pH

a little acid or base

Conductivity

a salt, e.g. KCl

Radioactivity

a radioisotope

The experiment, drawn

Tracer in at the inlet, detector at the outlet

$t_0$: injection; $t_1$: first tracer at the detector; $t_2$: last tracer leaves.

The tracer is chosen; now decide how to feed it.

Nonreactive tracer

Four ways to disturb the inlet

  • A nonreactive tracer only labels the fluid; it never changes the flow.
  • Periodic and random inputs are harder to interpret, so we use pulse and step.

The two tests used in this chapter

Pulse input or step input

Pulse: inject a mass $M$ all at once at $t_0$ into flow $v$. Used more often — one small dose gives the whole curve.
Step: at $t_0$ switch the feed to tracer at $C_{max}$, fed at $\dot m=C_{max}v$, and keep it on.
$M$
tracer mass injected in the pulse
kg or mol
$\dot m$
tracer feed rate in the step
kg/s
$C_{max}$
tracer level fed in the step
kg/m³
$C_{\text{pulse}},\ C_{\text{step}}$
outlet tracer concentration in each test
kg/m³
$v$
volumetric flow rate
m³/s

Ideal responses · red dashed line at $\bar t=V/v$

Plug flow, mixed flow, and a real vessel

Pulse inputStep inputWhat it means
Plug flowone age only: no distribution
Mixed flowoutlet = contents: tracer leaves at once
Real vessela spread of ages around $\bar t$

Response curve · time origin

Measure every age from the moment of injection

$$\text{residence time}=\bar t-t_0=\frac{V}{v}$$
  • Subtract $t_0$ from every reading, so injection is $t=0$.
  • Nothing leaves before $t_1$; the last tracer leaves at $t_2$.

Lecture 11-2

What section 11-2 settled

  • A nonreactive tracer labels the fluid; a detector at the exit records the response.
  • Pulse: inject $M$ at once. Step: switch to $C_{max}$ and hold it. Pulse is used more often.
  • Plug flow returns a delayed copy of the input; mixed flow responds at once and decays.
  • Timing and shape of a real response point to dead zones, bypass or recirculation.

Lecture 11-3

How do we determine the RTD by a pulse input of tracer?

Pulse set-upArea, mean and EExample 1

Lecture 11-3

From a pulse trace to E and $\bar t$

  1. The pulse experimentInject $M$ at once, record $C_{\text{pulse}}(t)$ at the exit.
  2. Area, mean and EArea gives $M/v$, the mean gives $V/v$, rescaling gives E.
  3. The procedure in four stepsWhat to do, in order, at the bench.
  4. A worked pulse testExample 1, by formula and by table.

11-2 showed the two ways to feed tracer. Start with the pulse.

Pulse input

Inject $M$ at once, record $C_{\text{pulse}}(t)$ at the exit

$M$
tracer injected at $t=0$
kg or mol
$C_{\text{pulse}}$
tracer concentration in the outlet
kg/m³
$v$
steady volumetric flow
m³/s
$V$
vessel volume
m³

Area, mean and spread of the C curve

What the trace tells you directly step 1 of 2

$$A=\int_0^\infty C\,dt\cong\sum_i C_i\Delta t_i=\frac{M}{v}$$
all tracer leaves: $\int vC\,dt=M$
$$\bar t=\frac{\int_0^\infty tC\,dt}{\int_0^\infty C\,dt}\cong\frac{\sum t_iC_i\Delta t_i}{\sum C_i\Delta t_i}=\frac{V}{v}$$
balance point of the trace; closed vessel
$$\sigma^2=\frac{\int_0^\infty (t-\bar t)^2C\,dt}{\int_0^\infty C\,dt}\cong\frac{\sum t_i^2C_i\Delta t_i}{\sum C_i\Delta t_i}-\bar t^2$$
spread about the mean, time²

$A$: area under the trace, kg·s/m³; $A\ne M/v$ means tracer was lost. $\sigma^2$: variance, s².

Rescale so the area is one

The C curve and the E curve step 2 of 2

$$A=\int_0^\infty C\,dt\cong\sum C_i\Delta t_i=\frac{M}{v}$$
units of $C$ × time, e.g. g·min/L
$$\mathbf E=\frac{C_{\text{pulse}}}{M/v}\ \Rightarrow\ \int_0^\infty\mathbf E\,dt=\frac{A}{M/v}=1$$
same shape, area one; E in min⁻¹
$$\bar t=\int_0^\infty t\,\mathbf E\,dt\cong\sum t_i\mathbf E_i\Delta t_i,\quad \sigma^2=\int_0^\infty t^2\mathbf E\,dt-\bar t^2\cong\sum t_i^2\mathbf E_i\Delta t_i-\bar t^2$$
area is 1: no division

Pulse input · at the bench

Determine the RTD by a pulse in four steps

1Inject $M$ at the inlet at $t=0$, in a time short against $\bar t$
→
2Record $C_{\text{pulse}}$ at the outlet until it returns to zero
→
3Check the area: $A=\sum C_i\Delta t_i$ must equal $M/v$
→
4Compute $\mathbf E_i=C_i/A$ and $\bar t=\dfrac{\sum t_iC_i\Delta t_i}{\sum C_i\Delta t_i}$

Step 3 is the quality check: tracer lost, adsorbed or not measured shows up as $A<M/v$.

Interactive 3 · virtual pulse test on a 150 L vessel

Change the dose and the flow: what moves?

Steps 1–2$A=M/v,\quad \bar t=V/v,\quad \mathbf E=C/(M/v)$
area $A$–
$\bar t$ from trace–
$V=\bar t\,v$–

Doubling $M$ doubles the trace but not E; changing $v$ moves $\bar t$, yet $\bar t\,v$ always returns the same 150 L.

Lecture 11-3

What section 11-3 settled

  • A pulse puts $M$ in at once; the outlet trace $C_{\text{pulse}}(t)$ is recorded until it returns to zero.
  • Area $A=M/v$ checks the test; the mean $\bar t=V/v$ sizes the vessel.
  • $\mathbf E=C_{\text{pulse}}/A$: always check that E has area one before using it.

Lecture 11-4

How do we determine the RTD by a step input of tracer?

Step set-upF from the step responseMean and E from FExample 2

Lecture 11-4

From a step response to F, E and $\bar t$

  1. The step experimentSwitch the feed to tracer at $t=0$ and keep it on.
  2. From $C_{\text{step}}$ to FDivide by the final level; F is the running area of E.
  3. $\bar t$ and E from FArea above F, slope of F.
  4. The procedure in four stepsWhat to do, in order, at the bench.
  5. A worked step testExample 2, with the integral done by table.

A pulse gives E directly. A step gives its running total.

Step input

Switch to tracer at $t=0$ and keep it on

$\dot m$
tracer feed rate after $t=0$
kg/s
$C_{\text{step}}$
outlet tracer concentration
kg/m³
$C_{max}$
final outlet level, $=\dot m/v$
kg/m³
$$C_{max}=\frac{\dot m}{v},\qquad \bar t=\frac{1}{C_{max}}\int_0^{C_{max}}t\,dC_{\text{step}}$$

Reading the step curve

Why the area above the step curve gives $\bar t$

$$\bar t=\frac{1}{C_{max}}\int_0^{C_{max}}t\,dC_{\text{step}}=\frac{\text{shaded area}}{C_{max}}$$
$$\frac{dC}{C_{max}}$$
rise $dC$ at time $t$ = new fluid of age $t$
$$\bar t=\int t\,\frac{dC}{C_{max}}$$
mean age: each age × its fraction, summed
$$t\,dC=\text{one strip}$$
all strips together fill the shaded area

Make the step dimensionless

$C_{\text{step}}$ becomes F, and F is the running area of E

$$\mathbf F(t)=\frac{C_{\text{step}}(t)}{C_{max}},\qquad 0\le\mathbf F\le1$$
fraction of the exit stream that is new, tracer-carrying fluid
$$\mathbf F(t)=\int_0^t\mathbf E\,dt$$
new fluid at the exit is fluid younger than $t$
$$\mathbf E=\frac{d\mathbf F}{dt}$$
differentiate both sides

F has no units; E has units of time⁻¹. 11-5 reads both curves in full.

Step data

Readings → F → E and $\bar t$

Previous slide$\mathbf F=C_{\text{step}}/C_{max},\quad \mathbf E=d\mathbf F/dt$
$$\bar t=\int_0^1 t\,d\mathbf F\cong\sum t_{mid,i}\,\Delta\mathbf F_i,\qquad t_{mid,i}=\frac{t_{i-1}+t_i}{2}$$
each $\Delta$F leaves during its interval: next slide
$$\mathbf E_i\cong\frac{\Delta\mathbf F_i}{\Delta t_i}$$
slope of F over each interval

Shift time so $t=0$ when tracer first appears, then add that offset back.

Step data come as readings of F. Which time multiplies each $\Delta$F?

Step data · the interval midpoint

$\Delta$F leaves during an interval, so read its time at the middle

  • Pulse (Example 1): $C_i$ is a reading at $t_i$; its bar is centred on $t_i$, so use $t_i$.
  • Step: $\Delta\mathbf F_i$ is what left between $t_{i-1}$ and $t_i$; use $t_{mid,i}=\tfrac{t_{i-1}+t_i}{2}$.
  • $\sum t_{mid}\Delta\mathbf F$ equals the area above F with the points joined by straight lines.
Proof: $V/v=40$ min, step readings every 20 min (Class Activity Problem I, N1)
time usedstart $t_{i-1}$middle $t_{mid}$end $t_i$
$\bar t$ (min)28.939.449.9

End or start shifts $\bar t$ by about $\Delta t/2$; the coarser the sampling, the bigger the error.

Interactive 4 · virtual step test

The area above F is the mean residence time

Previous slides$\bar t=\int_0^1 t\,d\mathbf F,\quad \mathbf E=d\mathbf F/dt$
grey area above F–
$t$ at $\mathbf F=0.5$–
peak of E–

Whatever the spread, the grey area stays equal to $\bar t$; a narrow spread only makes F rise steeply and E peak tall.

Step input · at the bench

Determine the RTD by a step in four steps

1At $t=0$ switch the feed to tracer at a steady rate $\dot m$ and hold it
→
2Record $C_{\text{step}}$ at the outlet until it levels at $C_{max}=\dot m/v$
→
3Divide every reading by $C_{max}$: $\mathbf F_i=C_i/C_{max}$
→
4Compute $\bar t\cong\sum t_{mid}\Delta\mathbf F_i$ and $\mathbf E_i\cong\Delta\mathbf F_i/\Delta t_i$

Read the tail finely: late readings carry large $t$, so a coarse tail biases $\bar t$.

Pulse, step, E, F and $\bar t$ together

From a pulseFrom a stepLinking them

$\mathbf F$ is dimensionless; $\mathbf E$ has units of time⁻¹.

Lecture 11-4

What section 11-4 settled

  • A step switches the feed to tracer at $t=0$ and holds it; the outlet rises to $C_{max}=\dot m/v$.
  • $\mathbf F=C_{\text{step}}/C_{max}$ is the running area of E, so $\mathbf E=d\mathbf F/dt$.
  • $\bar t=\int_0^1 t\,d\mathbf F\cong\sum t_{mid}\Delta\mathbf F_i$ (interval midpoints): the area above F.
  • E from step data needs a slope, so sample the steep part and the tail finely.

11-5

Lecture 11-5

What do the E, F and Eθ curves mean?

E: how many leave at each ageF: how many have left by tEθ: the pattern without the size

Lecture 11-5

Three curves, one residence time distribution

  1. The E curveExit ages, normalisation, younger and older fractions.
  2. Mean and spread$\bar t$ locates the curve; the variance measures its width.
  3. E for the two idealsA spike for plug flow, a decaying exponential for mixed.
  4. $\mathbf E_\theta$ and the F curveSize removed; ages accumulated.
  5. Reading all three togetherOne vessel, three curves, one story.

11-3 and 11-4 turned outlet readings into E and F. Now we give each one a precise meaning.

Definition

The exit age distribution, E

$t$
age: time an exit element spent in the vessel
s
$\mathbf E(t)$
exit age distribution = the RTD
s⁻¹
$\mathbf E\,dt$
fraction of exit stream with age $t$ to $t+dt$
–
$$\int_0^\infty \mathbf E\,dt=1$$

Normalised: every element of the exit stream has some age.

$\mathbf E$ carries units of time⁻¹ so that $\mathbf E\,dt$ is a pure fraction.

Condition behind E

E is defined for fluid that enters once and leaves once

  • Closed: each element has one age, so the measured curve $=\mathbf E$, $\int_0^\infty\mathbf E\,dt=1$ and $\bar t=V/v$.
  • Open: an element can cross the exit twice, so the measured curve $\ne\mathbf E$ and $\bar t>V/v$.
  • Most reactors with small inlet and outlet pipes behave as closed vessels.

The tracer relations of 11-3 and 11-4 assume a closed vessel.

Reading areas under E · Eqs. 1–2

How much of the exit stream left before $t_1$?

$$\text{fraction younger than }t_1=\int_0^{t_1}\mathbf E\,dt$$
add every age slice from zero to $t_1$
$$\text{fraction older than }t_1=\int_{t_1}^{\infty}\mathbf E\,dt=1-\int_0^{t_1}\mathbf E\,dt$$
total area is one, so the rest is older

$t_1$ is any chosen age, s. Both fractions are dimensionless.

Interactive 5 · areas under the RTD

Move $t_1$ and read the two fractions

From the previous slide$\int_0^{t_1}\mathbf E\,dt+\int_{t_1}^{\infty}\mathbf E\,dt=1$
younger than $t_1$–
older (shaded)–

At $t_1=\bar t=15$ min only 37 % of the mixed tank’s exit is older than the mean; the less skewed measured vessel gives 48 %.

Areas gave fractions. The balance point of the curve gives one number for the whole stream.

First moment of E

The mean residence time $\bar t$

$$\bar t=\int_0^\infty t\,\mathbf E\,dt=\frac{V}{v}$$

The age-weighted average of the exit stream.

$=V/v$ only for a closed vessel with no density change; 11-3 proves it.

$\bar t$
mean residence time
s
$V$
volume of the vessel holding the fluid
m³
$v$
volumetric flow rate through it
m³/s

Second moment of E

How wide is the distribution? The variance

$$\sigma^2=\int_0^\infty (t-\bar t)^2\mathbf E\,dt\cong\frac{\sum (t_i-\bar t)^2C_i\Delta t_i}{\sum C_i\Delta t_i}$$
$\sigma^2$
variance: spread of ages about $\bar t$
s²

Plug flow: $\sigma^2=0$. The wider the spread of ages, the larger $\sigma^2$.

Ideal 1 · Eqs. 17–19

Plug flow: every element has age $\bar t$

$$\mathbf E_{\text{plug}}=\delta(t-\bar t)$$

An infinitely tall spike of zero width at $t_0=\bar t$, with area one.

Delta rules: $\int_0^\infty\delta(t-t_0)\,dt=1$ and $\int_0^\infty\delta(t-t_0)f(t)\,dt=f(t_0)$: the spike picks out one value.

Ideal 2 · derived, not quoted

Mixed flow: why E decays exponentially step 1 of 2

$$V\frac{dC}{dt}=0-vC$$
tracer balance after a pulse; outlet = contents
$$\frac{dC}{dt}=-\frac{C}{\bar t}\;\Rightarrow\;C=C_0\,e^{-t/\bar t}$$
divide by $V$; $\bar t=V/v$; integrate from $C_0$

$C$: tracer concentration in tank and outlet, kg/m³; $C_0=M/V$ just after injecting $M$ kg.

Ideal 2 · normalise

Mixed flow: why E decays exponentially step 2 of 2

$$\int_0^\infty C\,dt=C_0\bar t$$
area of the exponential
$$\mathbf E_{\text{mixed}}=\frac{C}{C_0\bar t}=\frac{1}{\bar t}\,e^{-t/\bar t}$$
divide by the area so it becomes one

Valid for one ideal stirred tank; youngest fluid is the most common age.

Why a dimensionless RTD

Measure time in units of $\bar t$: one curve per flow pattern

$$\theta=\frac{t}{\bar t},\quad \mathbf E_\theta=\bar t\,\mathbf E,\quad \sigma_\theta^2=\frac{\sigma^2}{\bar t^{\,2}}$$

$\theta$, $\mathbf E_\theta$, $\sigma_\theta^2$: dimensionless age, RTD, variance.

  • Compare sizes: same flow pattern, any $\bar t$ → one $\mathbf E_\theta$ (lab to plant).
  • Shape only: area 1, mean 1; the spread $\sigma_\theta^2$ tells the pattern: plug flow 0, one mixed tank 1.
  • Models (dispersion, tanks in series) are written in $\theta$.

Interactive 6 · same design, different size

Change $\bar t$: E moves, $\mathbf E_\theta$ does not

From the previous slide$\theta=t/\bar t,\ \ \mathbf E_\theta=\bar t\,\mathbf E,\ \ \sigma_\theta^2=\sigma^2/\bar t^{\,2}$
peak of E–
peak of Eθ–
σ² of E–
σθ² of Eθ–

Shape: the measured vessel of Example 1, scaled. Dashed grey: $\bar t=15$ min.

E vs t
Eθ vs θ

Doubling $\bar t$ halves the E peak and makes $\sigma^2$ four times larger, while $\mathbf E_\theta$ and $\sigma_\theta^2$ stay put — they describe the flow pattern, not the size.

Fig. 11.12

Make the step dimensionless: the F curve

$$\mathbf F=\frac{C_{\text{step}}}{C_{max}}=\frac{v}{\dot m}\,C_{\text{step}}$$

$\mathbf F$ rises from 0 to 1; dimensionless.

Area above the F curve $=\bar t$, in seconds.

Imagine white fluid, switched to red at $t=0$. At time $t$, only red fluid in the outlet is younger than $t$ — so $\mathbf F$ is the fraction of the exit younger than $t$.

Eqs. 7–8

F is the running area under E

$$\Big(\text{fraction red in exit}\Big)=\Big(\text{fraction of exit younger than }t\Big)$$
only fluid entering after $t=0$ is red
$$\mathbf F=\int_0^t\mathbf E\,dt$$
left = F; right = Eq. 1 with $t_1=t$
$$\frac{d\mathbf F}{dt}=\mathbf E$$
differentiate both sides

Like every tracer link here, this holds for closed vessels only.

Interactive 7 · E, F and $\mathbf E_\theta$ of the same vessel, $\bar t=15$ min

Move $t_1$ and read all three curves at once

$\mathbf F(t_1)$–
$\mathbf E(t_1)$–
$\theta_1$–
$\sigma_\theta^2$–

E: shaded area = F
F: running total
Eθ: size removed

The green area under E is the height of F, and $\mathbf E_\theta$ is the same shape on a $\theta$ axis: three views of one distribution.

The two ideals and a real vessel

E, F and Eθ for plug flow, mixed flow and a real vessel

Plug flow

$\mathbf E=\delta(t-\bar t)$
$\mathbf F=0$, then $1$ at $t=\bar t$
$\mathbf E_\theta=\delta(\theta-1)$, $\sigma_\theta^2=0$

Mixed flow

$\mathbf E=\frac1{\bar t}e^{-t/\bar t}$
$\mathbf F=1-e^{-t/\bar t}$
$\mathbf E_\theta=e^{-\theta}$, $\sigma_\theta^2=1$

Real vessel

$\mathbf E$: measured (11-3)
$\mathbf F=\int_0^t\mathbf E\,dt$ (11-4)
$\mathbf E_\theta=\bar t\,\mathbf E$, $0<\sigma_\theta^2<1$

A real vessel lies between the ideals: E a hump around $\bar t$, F an S-curve, $\mathbf E_\theta$ centred near $\theta=1$.

Three curves, defined and drawn. Here is what each one answers.

The meaning of E, F and $\mathbf E_\theta$

Three questions, three curves

E curve · min⁻¹

How much of the exit fluid has age $t$? Distribution: $\mathbf E\,dt$ is a fraction; area 1. From a pulse.

F curve · –

How much has stayed less than $t$? Cumulative: rises 0 to 1; $\mathbf F=\int\mathbf E\,dt$. From a step.

$\mathbf E_\theta$ curve · –

What is the flow pattern, whatever the size? Mean at $\theta=1$. Compares vessels and models.

What comes next

Read the measured E curve for faults

Where the volume goes

Active and dead volume, bypass and recycle. 11-6.

Reactor ills

Early, late, split or repeating curves, and their cures. 11-7.

Flow models

Dispersion and tanks in series, for vessels between the ideals.

Every diagnosis starts from the same three numbers: area, mean and variance.

Lecture 11-5

What section 11-5 settled

  • E: fraction of exit fluid per unit age, area one; F: fraction younger than $t$, $\mathbf F=\int_0^t\mathbf E\,dt$.
  • $\bar t=\int t\mathbf E\,dt=V/v$ locates the curve; $\sigma^2$ measures its spread.
  • Plug flow: $\delta(t-\bar t)$, $\sigma_\theta^2=0$. Mixed flow: $\frac1{\bar t}e^{-t/\bar t}$, $\sigma_\theta^2=1$.
  • $\mathbf E_\theta=\bar t\,\mathbf E$ keeps the flow pattern and drops the size.

11-6

Lecture 11-6

Where has the volume gone? Active volume, dead volume and bypass

Active & dead volumeBypass & recycle flowTwo checks before any diagnosis

Lecture 11-6

What a tracer curve can tell about the volume

  1. How long, not whereThe RTD gives ages; the regions must be inferred.
  2. Active and dead volume$V=V_a+V_d$, and what each region does to a pulse.
  3. Active, bypass and recycle flowWhat each stream does to a pulse.
  4. Two checksTracer balance, then $\bar t_{obs}$ against $V/v$ to size the dead volume.

11-2 to 11-5 measured the exit age distribution E(t) with a tracer.

How long, not where

The RTD says how long fluid stays — not where

Active, dead or bypassed: where fluid goes is inferred from the shape and mean of E.

Recall Lecture 10 · slides 7 and 8

Every real reactor leans towards one of the two ideals

near plug flow
near mixed flow

None is exactly ideal. The tracer curve shows how far each one drifts, and why.

Three kinds of volume

Not all of the vessel volume is in use

$$V = V_p + V_m + V_d$$
$$V_a = V_p + V_m$$

Only the active volume $V_a$ ever sees the flowing fluid.

$V$
total volume of the vessel
m³
$V_p$
plug-flow region
m³
$V_m$
mixed-flow region
m³
$V_d$
dead or stagnant region
m³
$V_a$
active volume
m³

Three kinds of flow

Split the throughflow into three streams

$$v = v_a + v_b$$

$v_r$ circulates inside the vessel: it adds passes, not throughput.

$v$
total volumetric flow
m³/s
$v_a$
active flow, through $V_p$ and $V_m$
m³/s
$v_b$
bypass flow, inlet straight to outlet
m³/s
$v_r$
recycle flow, outlet region back to inlet
m³/s

Three kinds of volume

What each region does to a pulse of tracer

Plug region

Delays the pulse by $V_p/v$; shape kept.

Mixed region

Spreads it into a decay of mean $V_m/v$.

Dead region

Never reached, so the mean comes early.

Three kinds of flow

What each extra stream does to a pulse

Bypass $v_b$

A spike at $t\approx0$ holding the fraction $v_b/v$ of the tracer.

Recycle $v_r$

The pulse comes round again: a train of shrinking peaks.

Interactive 8 · dead volume and bypass in action

Add dead volume or bypass, then watch the curve

t̄obs ÷ V/v–

With 20 % dead volume the mean arrives at 0.80 V/v whatever the plug share; a bypass adds a spike at zero.

What must be measured · check 1

Does the tracer balance close?

From 11-3$M = v\displaystyle\int_0^\infty C\,dt$$\bar t_{obs}=\dfrac{\int_0^\infty t\,C\,dt}{\int_0^\infty C\,dt}$
  • $M$ and $C$ in real units: the area under C must equal $M/v$. Less area means tracer was lost (adsorbed, leaked) or a reading is off: fix the test first.
  • Only a relative signal (e.g. conductivity, arbitrary units): the area cannot be compared with $M/v$, so the balance cannot be checked.
  • $\bar t_{obs}$ is found either way: scaling every $C$ by the same factor scales top and bottom of the ratio alike, so it cancels.

$M$: tracer injected, kg · $C$: outlet concentration, kg/m³ · $\bar t_{obs}$: mean of the measured curve, s.

What must be measured · check 2

Is any of the volume dead?

$$\bar t=\frac{V}{v}\qquad \bar t_{obs}=\frac{V_a}{v}$$

Tracer only ever fills $V_a$, so the curve measures $V_a$ — not $V$.

MeasuredMeaning
$\bar t_{obs}<\bar t$dead regions exist
$\bar t_{obs}=\bar t$no dead regions
$\bar t_{obs}>\bar t$impossible: recheck $v$, $V$, tracer

$V$ and $v$ must be measured independently of the tracer test.

Interactive 9 · check 2 in numbers

Find the dead volume from $\bar t_{obs}$

From the previous slide$V_a=v\,\bar t_{obs},\quad V_d=V-V_a$
$V/v$–
$V_a$–
$V_d$–
dead–

The same $\bar t_{obs}=3$ min means 25 % dead in a 6 m³ vessel — and none if $V$ were 4.5 m³.

Lecture 11-6

What section 11-6 settled

  • Only the active volume $V_a=V-V_d$ is swept; the tracer measures $\bar t_{obs}=V_a/v$.
  • Plug delays a pulse, mixed spreads it, bypass spikes it at zero, recycle repeats it.
  • Check first: area $=M/v$; then $V_d=V-v\,\bar t_{obs}$.
  • Dead volume shows only as $\bar t_{obs}<V/v$ — so $V$ and $v$ must be measured too.

Lecture 11-7 · diagnosing reactor ills

A reactor underperforms — what does its tracer curve say is wrong, and what should we fix?

Pulse & step testsMisbehaving plug-flow reactorsMisbehaving mixed-flow reactorsLecture 10’s reactors on the bench

Lecture 11-7

Read the fault from the curve, then confirm it

  1. Run the testPulse or step, into ideal plug and mixed flow first.
  2. Misbehaving plug-flow reactorsEarly, late, double and repeating peaks (Fig. 12.3).
  3. Misbehaving mixed-flow reactorsLags, early spikes, slow circulation (Fig. 12.4).
  4. Lecture 10’s reactors on the benchFixed and trickle beds, loops, tanks, fluidized beds, airlifts.
  5. Find the faultA closed vessel to diagnose from its outlet alone.

Run the test

Two ways to feed tracer, two curves

Pulse input

Inject a dose $M$ at once. The outlet traces E: when each element leaves.

11-3$\mathbf E=\dfrac{C_{pulse}}{M/v}$

Step input

Switch the feed to tracer at $t=0$. The outlet traces F: the running area of E.

11-4$\mathbf F=\dfrac{C_{step}}{C_0}=\displaystyle\int_0^t\mathbf E\,dt$

Interactive 10 · tracer test on the two ideals

Feed tracer into ideal plug flow and ideal mixed flow

t̄obs ÷ V/v–

Same mean, opposite extremes: plug flow returns the pulse as one spike at V/v; the mixed tank answers at once and decays.

Misbehaving plug-flow reactors · Fig. 12.3, 1 of 2

Healthy, early, or recirculating

Slim, mean in placereasonably good plug flow
Mean too earlystagnant backwaters; the long tail is easily missed
Peaks at regular intervalsstrong internal recirculation

Misbehaving plug-flow reactors · Fig. 12.3, 2 of 2

Double peaks, and a curve that arrives late

Double peakparallel paths: speedy and slow fluid, channeling
Late curvethe balance says it cannot happen
So one of these holds:
  • $v$ or $V$ measured wrongly
  • tracer not inert — it adsorbs
  • the vessel is not closed

Interactive 11 · Lecture 10’s plug-type reactors on the test bench

Make a bed misbehave, then read its tracer curve

t̄obs ÷ V/v–

Each fault leaves its own mark: a channel splits the peak, stagnant pockets pull the mean early, an adsorbing tracer pushes it late.

Misbehaving mixed-flow reactors · Fig. 12.4, 1 of 2

Healthy, delayed, or slowly circulating

Decay, mean in placereasonably good mixing
Time lagplug flow in series: a long inlet pipe or sampling line
Bumps on the decayslow internal circulation, a draft-tube effect

Misbehaving mixed-flow reactors · Fig. 12.4, 2 of 2

Early, late, or short-circuited

Early meanstagnant fluid in the tank
Late meanwrong $v$ or $V$, or a tracer that is not inert
Sharp early peakshort-circuiting from inlet to outlet

Interactive 12 · Lecture 10’s well-mixed reactors on the test bench

Make a tank misbehave, then read its tracer curve

t̄obs ÷ V/v–

A short-circuit spikes at zero, a long inlet line delays the decay, slow circulation rides fading bumps on it, and an adsorbing tracer pushes the mean late.

The vessel is closed: diagnose it from its outlet

t̄obs ÷ V/v–

With the inside hidden, only the curve is left — exactly the position of the engineer at the plant.

A diagnosis is only useful if it points at something to change.

Diagnosing reactor ills

From symptom to cure

Curve showsLikely causeWhat to do
Early meandead or stagnant zonesstronger agitation, baffles, fill corners
Sharp spike near zeroshort-circuit, bypassmove or redirect the inlet
Double peakchanneling in a bedrepack, improve the distributor
Regular repeating peaksinternal recirculationexpect mixed-flow behaviour, or break the loop
Lag, then decayplug flow in seriesshorten lines; model it, it may be harmless
Late meanwrong $v$, $V$ or tracerrecalibrate; use an inert tracer

Lecture 11-7

What section 11-7 settled

  • A pulse gives E; a step gives F, the running area of E.
  • Early mean: dead zones. Spike near zero: short-circuit. Double peak: channeling.
  • Repeating peaks: recirculation. Lag: plug flow in series. Late mean: a measurement fault.
  • Check the balance and the mean first — they decide which faults are possible.

Problem I (Part A Problem I of Final Exam 2024) · 1 of 2 · read it all before we start

Mixed flow reactor: aspirin in a 5000 L stirred tank

A 5000 L industrial stirred-tank reactor is used to produce aspirin through the following main reaction. A side reaction also occurs between salicylic acid (SA) and acetic acid (HA).

Recently, reaction kinetics were re-evaluated using a 10 L stirred-tank reactor. The apparent rate law was found to change from first-order (previous result) to third-order kinetics, described by the following rate law: $r_{app}=kC_{SA}^{3}$, $k=5.87\ \text{L}^6/(\text{mol}^2\cdot\text{min})$. This reaction rate law is now applied to estimate the residence time in an industrial-scale 5000 L reactor.

To validate the non-ideal flow behavior in the 5000 L reactor, the effect of rotational speed on performance was investigated. The reactor is designed for continuous flow operation. A series of tracer experiments was conducted at two different agitator speeds, 120 rpm and 180 rpm, as summarized in the table on the next slide.

The liquid feed stream matches the reactant feed, with a flow rate of 125 L/min, and the initial and feed concentrations of salicylic acid are controlled at 1 mol/L.

Calculate the rotational speed of the impeller if the power per unit volume (P/V) is 0.50 kW/m³. Assume the solution properties are similar to water (density 1000 kg/m³, viscosity 1 cP).

Problem I · sub-question 3 · step 1 of 5

C curve: pulse input or step input?

Think first: a pulse comes out as a hump that returns to zero; a step rises and stays. Which is this?

Plot C against t for both speeds and look at the end of the curve.

Step input. C rises from 0 and levels at $C_{max}=80$ mg/mL; it never returns to zero.

  • A pulse would give a peak with area $M/v$, then C → 0.
  • So the data are a running total: divide by $C_{max}$ to get F.

Problem II (Part A Problem 1 of Final Exam 2023) · 1 of 2 · read it all before we start

Fixed-bed tube: o-xylene to phthalic anhydride

Partial oxidation of o-xylene in air for the phthalic anhydride production process follows the reaction shown. These strongly exothermic processes are carried out in multitubular reactors cooled by molten salt circulating around the tubes, which exchanges heat to an internal or external boiler.

Reactor dimension. The tubes are 3 m long with an internal diameter of 2.54 cm. The reactor operates isothermally at 350 °C.

Catalyst. V₂O₅ on promoted silica gel, effective spherical diameter 5 mm, particle density 1,300 kg/m³, bed void fraction 0.43.

Feed. Nearly atmospheric (1 bar). Partial pressures: N₂ 0.772 bar, O₂ 0.21 bar, o-xylene 0.018 bar, kept below 1 mol% to stay under the explosion limit. Superficial gas velocity 0.30 m/s; 2500 tubes give 1650 tons/yr.

Kinetics at 350 °C: $r_{app}=k_1P_{xylene}$, $k_1=0.23\ \text{mol}/(\text{s}\cdot\text{m}^3_{bed}\cdot\text{bar})$.

Fluid properties. Diffusivity of xylene in the catalyst pore 5×10⁻⁵ m²/s; gas viscosity 0.01 cP; gas density 0.57 kg/m³. Hint: bed density = (1 − void) × particle density.

Problem III (Part A Problem 1 of Final Exam 2022) · 1 of 2 · read it all before we start

Stirred tank: aspirin at two agitator speeds

The 5000 L industrial stirred-tank reactor was used to produce aspirin by the following main reaction. A side reaction was also found between SA and HA.

From the kinetic study in the lab-scale 20 L reactor, the apparent rate law $r_{app}=k_1C_{SA}$, $k_1=0.112\ \text{min}^{-1}$, was obtained and used to design a 5000 L reactor.

To validate the non-ideal flow, the effect of rotational speed in the 5000 L reactor was investigated. The unit is designed for continuous flow operation. To determine whether its performance approximated an ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor, tracer experiments were carried out at 120 and 150 rpm.

The response of a non-reacting system to a pulse of tracer injected into a steadily flowing liquid stream at 60 L/min was used to characterise the reactor. The data are on the next slide.

Problem V · sub-question 1.1–1.2 · step 1 of 5

C curve: pulse input or step input?

Think first: a pulse comes out as a hump that returns to zero; a step rises and stays. Which is this?

Plot C against t and look at the end of the curve.

Step input. C rises from 0 and levels at $C_{max}$ = 7.7 g/cm³; it never returns to zero.

  • The data are a running total: divide by $C_{max}$ to get F.
  • The flow rate is not given: the tracer has to tell us $\bar t$, then $v=V/\bar t$.

Lecture 11

Key Takeaways

1

Characterise a real vessel by its RTD, measured with a nonreactive tracer.

2

Check every test: area $=M/v$, $\bar t=V/v$, and E integrates to one.

3

Read E as a distribution, F as its running total, $\mathbf E_\theta$ as the pattern without the size.

4

Diagnose from the response: dead zones lower $\bar t$, bypass spikes early, recirculation repeats.

5

Size the dead volume from $\bar t_{obs}$ against $V/v$, read bypass, channels and recirculation from the shape, then fix the fault.
